text: Beginners often picture machine learning as pick an algorithm, call fit, done. In practice the algorithm is a small part of the job. Professional data scientists spend most of their time on the steps around the model — framing the question, preparing data, and checking honestly whether the result is any good. This lesson gives you the map of the whole workflow.

Six stages. Frame the problem — what decision will the prediction support, what's the target, pick a metric before you touch a model. Get and explore the data — check types, missing values, distributions. Prepare the data — split, clean, encode, scale, engineer features, the biggest source of hidden mistakes. Train models, starting with a simple baseline. Evaluate on data the model has never seen. And deploy and monitor, watching for drift as the world changes.

Real projects loop — a poor evaluation sends you back to features, or even back to reframing the problem entirely. Let's see an honest minimal version using scikit-learn's bundled breast-cancer dataset — 569 tumours, 30 measurements each, labeled benign or malignant.

Splitting the data, then fitting a baseline, a logistic regression, and a random forest, all scored only on held-out test rows: the baseline, which always answers benign, scores 62.9 percent. Logistic regression and random forest both score 95.8 percent.

This output teaches three things. First, the baseline matters — 62.7 percent of tumours are benign, so a model that always says benign already scores 62.9 percent. Any real model must beat that, and knowing the baseline stops you being impressed by a mediocre number, especially when classes are imbalanced like this.

Second, the split protects you — every model was fit only on the training rows and scored only on rows it never saw. Scoring on training rows would flatter the model, and lessons 4 and 5 show exactly why. Third, one number isn't the whole story — both real models tie at 95.8 percent, but for a medical screen, missing a malignant tumour is worse than a false alarm, so you'd look at the kinds of errors, not just accuracy.

Choosing the right metric is part of framing the problem, not an afterthought. The test set is a one-shot exam — if you try ten models, tweak features, and pick whichever scores best on the test set, you've quietly trained on it, and its score is no longer honest.

In Lesson 7 you'll meet the validation set, which is exactly where all that experimenting belongs instead. To recap: an ML project is a loop of framing, data work, modeling, and honest evaluation, with the model itself a small piece. Set a metric and a baseline first, split before you experiment, and only trust scores from data the model has not seen. Next up, lesson 4: bias, variance, and generalization.
